title: Śrīdhara Svāmī literal English — Canto 4, chapter 4, complete checkpoint
source_note: Rendered only the thirty-four Śrīdhara Svāmī glosses in the pinned Sanskrit file, in their actual verse order. The verses include Satī's rebuke and her account of giving up her body; rendering them records the historical commentary, not a present-day instruction or endorsement. Source checking here does not amount to independent collation of the 1949 printed scan or live browser testing.

entries.text: In the fourth chapter she leaves her husband and goes; insulted by her father at the sacrifice, she rebukes him in anger and abandons her body. ‘In either case’ means both if permission were given and if she were forcibly restrained. Wishing to see her friends, she was going out; apprehensive of Bhava, she went back in again. Thus Satī was of two minds: she neither went nor remained, but moved as though on a swing.

‘Distressed’ means distressed by the obstruction of her wish to see her friends. She was greatly agitated by small drops of tears. ‘Without an equal person’ means one who has no other person equal to himself. ‘As though she would burn him’ means as though she would reduce him to ashes; trembling had arisen in her from anger.

Then, leaving him, she went to her parents' house. What was he like? Out of love he had given her half of his own body. The reason for her leaving was that her understanding was bewildered by womanly nature, the disposition of a woman.

‘Of swift stride’ means going quickly. They were accompanied by attendants and Yakṣas. Maṇimān and Mada were foremost among them. The chief bull went in front of them. ‘Free from distress’ means without affliction; alternatively, they were afflicted on account of her going in defiance of Rudra.

Having mounted her upon the chief bull, they went, adorned with playthings such as the sārikā bird and with royal insignia such as a white parasol. A sārikā is the bird described as being taught to recite. ‘With song-receptacles’ means with things that serve as the supports of song.

The sacrificial place was splendid with Vedic recitation sounding all around and was the site of the dismemberment of sacrificial animals. Or its sacrificial commotion, the mutual rivalry there, was heightened by the recitation. The goddess entered that sacrificial place, frequented also by the gods, in which vessels and implements had been fashioned from clay and the other materials mentioned.

‘No one honored her’ means no one received her with honor, out of fear of Dakṣa, the sacrificer. The reason was that he had dishonored her. ‘Except her sisters and mother’ means apart from them. They, however, embraced her respectfully and gladly; their throats were choked by tears of love.

Satī, not welcomed, that is, not honored by her father, did not accept the offering. How so? Along with it came conversation suitable to the greetings of sisters by reason of their sharing the same womb. She did not accept even that: she did not listen to it. This is the meaning.
She saw the sacrifice in which no portion for Rudra existed. The insult done to the deity Rudra was the failure to invite him and the like.

‘She rebuked’ means she censured him. Her speech was impaired and indistinct through indignation, through anger. ‘A hater of Śiva’ means one who hates Śiva. The path of smoke is the path of ritual action; the practice of it had made him proud. She restrained, that is, prevented, by her own command the hosts of beings that had risen to kill Dakṣa.

She continues her censure in thirteen verses. ‘Free from enmity’ means having abandoned opposition. Who other than you would act against that Śiva? The causes of his lack of enmity are these: no one in the world is superior to him, and he has neither a favored nor a disfavored person. Under the compound reading, no one is exceedingly dear to him. He is the self dear to embodied beings. He is the self of all, their cause, or he has the form of all.

Acting against him is of two kinds: hostility to the greatest persons and hostility directly to him. Explaining four kinds of people, she speaks of hostility to the greatest in the two verses beginning ‘Faults.’ ‘O twice-born’ is a reproach. Envious people such as you take only faults in the virtues of others, not virtues. Some, who stand in the middle, do not take faults in virtues but discern virtues and faults as they stand; they are called great. Good people take virtues alone and not faults; they are greater. The greatest do not take faults at all; instead they magnify even slight, insignificant virtues. You have ‘found a fault’ among them: that is, you have perceived or imagined one. This was indicated by ‘having disregarded those established in Brahman’ [4.3.3].

This is indeed fitting among wicked people, as she says with ‘Not.’ They are people who call the inert body, a corpse, their very self. Envy means inability to bear another's good. That such people continually revile the great with envy is not surprising. Alternatively, their brilliance and influence have been cast down through envy by the dust of the feet of great persons. Though great persons tolerate their own censure, the dust of their feet does not tolerate it and destroys the offenders' influence. Thus the reviling of the great is characteristic of those who have no strength: this is the meaning.

Having described hostility toward the greatest persons, she speaks in two verses of hostility done to him directly. That well-known name of his, consisting of just two syllables, ‘Śiva,’ quickly destroys all the sin of people. It need only be uttered with the voice, not with a preceding act of thought, and even once, even incidentally. You hate that Śiva, whose fame is purifying and whose command cannot be transgressed. Ah! ‘Other than auspicious’ means having the form of inauspiciousness.

Having stated that he removes sin, she describes Śiva as granting enjoyment and liberation. The lotus of his feet is attended by the bees that are the minds of the great, desirous of nectar that is the relish of Brahman, the bliss of Brahman. That same lotus showers the various blessings sought by people who desire their objects.

She challenges the statements that he is ‘auspicious in name but inauspicious’ and that he dwells among the dead. He lives in the cremation ground with his matted hair scattered; its garlands, ashes and human skulls serve as his adornments. Do Brahmā and the others besides you not know him? If they knew, one might say, their serving him would make no sense if he were as you say. Yet they carry upon their heads the cast-off offerings that have fallen from his feet.

Now, intending to give up her body, she states the principle of dharma. When the Lord, the guardian of dharma and master, is reviled by unrestrained persons, one should cover the ears and depart if one is not capable of dying or killing. If one has the power, the verse speaks of forcibly cutting out the harsh tongue that utters inauspicious words, and then even giving up one's own life. It calls this dharma.

‘Born from you’ means arisen from you. ‘The blue-throated one’ means the one whose throat is blue; you are his reviler. She gives an example to show that there is no purification without casting off an impure thing taken in through error: the expulsion of food that has been eaten is vomiting; that alone is said to purify a person.

She answers the charge that he is one whose rites are abandoned and who is unclean. The mind of the great sage who delights in his own self, who is completely detached, does not follow Vedic injunctions and prohibitions because his eligibility for them has ceased. The difference of eligibility is illustrated by the gods moving in the sky and human beings on earth. Therefore one who is established in one's own dharma, whether of active engagement or withdrawal, should not disparage the other dharma or a person established in it: because eligibility is distinct, both are valid. Alternatively, the construction is simply ‘should not disparage.’

She establishes this: engaged action such as agnihotra and withdrawn action such as tranquility and restraint are indeed true because they are enjoined in the Veda. They are prescribed distinctly, according to an arrangement, not indiscriminately. Both have a distinguishing mark that qualifies the eligible person: attachment and detachment. It may be asked whether ‘one should offer agnihotra throughout life’ and ‘one should be tranquil and restrained’ reveal no such division. True; nevertheless, since both cannot belong to the same eligibility, such a division is the resulting sense. The two actions contradict each other when they belong simultaneously to one agent. But should not Śiva then perform the withdrawn action? No action whatever reaches Brahman, Sadāśiva. Thus, just as the engaged and withdrawn do not incur a fault for failing to perform one another's duties, neither does the Lord incur a fault for performing neither.

She answers the charge that Śiva lacks enjoyment, inferred from his use of cremation ashes, nakedness and the like. O father, the paths or attainments such as aṇimā that we have taken up are not yours; they do not belong to you. Your paths are confined to sacrificial halls and are praised and enjoyed by those who follow the path of smoke and are satisfied only with the sacrificial food. Our paths are not of this sort: their grounds or causes are not manifest, since they arise from mere will, and they are served by avadhūtas, knowers of Brahman. Therefore do not be proud, thinking, ‘I am wealthy; Rudra is poor.’

Why say more? She declares in two verses that she will indeed abandon this body. Is this body arisen from you not sufficient? It is more than enough, because it is of bad birth: born from your body, you who have committed an offense against Hari. An objection arises: is not this body praiseworthy? No, she says, the connection with a base person, you, has caused me shame. Therefore shame on the birth that comes from one who does what is displeasing to the great. Through its connection with you, this body is not praiseworthy.

Even in jest, when the bull-bannered Lord addresses me as ‘Dākṣāyaṇī,’ taking up your lineage-name, the name that expresses my relation to you, I become exceedingly distressed, with my playful smile gone. Therefore, certainly, I shall cast off this body, which is like a corpse.

Having addressed Dakṣa at the sacrifice, she sat upon the ground facing north, O destroyer of enemies, that is, of foes such as anger. In another reading she was north-facing. ‘Speech stilled’ means observing silence; ‘having touched water’ means having sipped water for purification; ‘her eyes’ means her sight.

He explains the yogic course. Having made the two breaths, prāṇa and apāna, which move upward and downward, equal or one through restraint at the navel center, she raised udāna from there, placed it in the heart together with the understanding, and brought it through the throat to the space between the eyebrows.
‘The most venerable among the great’ means Śrī Rudra.
The nectar in the lotus of her husband's feet is the bliss of worship. She saw nothing other than her husband. Her body at once blazed up: the fire was the one produced through samādhi.
In the sky and on earth there arose the cry ‘Alas! Alas!’ and the like. He gives its words with ‘Ah!’—the cry was of sorrow: ‘Who, namely Dakṣa, angered the goddess who was dear to this deity?’

‘Great lack of self’ means great wickedness. They say that affection should indeed extend everywhere in his case, with ‘whose [creatures are all his offspring].’ ‘By whom she was disapproved’ means by whom she was scorned.

‘Whose heart is hard to endure’ means whose heart is exceedingly intolerant. ‘In the world’ means among people. From the word ‘and,’ he will also obtain hell. ‘Because’ means because he did not restrain his own daughter, born from his body, when she was ready to die on account of his offense, his own contempt toward her. ‘Hater of the Puruṣa’ means hater of Śiva.
‘Having seen the extraordinary thing,’ too.
‘That which kills the destroyers of sacrifice’ means that which destroys those who destroy the sacrifice; [the Yajurvedic formula begins] ‘Drive away the demon,’ and so forth.
The officiating priest was Bhṛgu. The gods named Ṛbhus, who had obtained Soma through austerity, arose.
‘Shining’ means blazing with brahminical power.
